nameStory: The name 'centaury' comes from the legendary centaur Chiron in Greek mythology, who was said to have used this plant to heal wounds with his knowledge of herbal medicine. The word 'common' distinguishes it from its smaller relative, lesser centaury, though both are actually quite uncommon in New England!
description: Common centaury is a delicate annual wildflower that grows 6-18 inches tall with bright pink, five-petaled flowers. This European native belongs to the gentian family and forms small, branching clusters of flowers atop slender stems. The plant has a neat, upright growth habit with pairs of oval leaves climbing up the stem, creating an orderly appearance that's quite charming when you spot one of these rare beauties.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright rose-pink flowers with exactly 5 petals arranged in flat, star-like clusters at the top of stems. Each flower is about half an inch across and closes up on cloudy days or in the evening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs up the stem, with 3-5 parallel veins running from base to tip. Leaves feel slightly thick and waxy to the touch, with no teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single-stemmed plant that branches near the top into a flat-topped flower cluster. The whole plant has a tidy, geometric appearance and stands 6-18 inches tall.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel firm and smooth, often with a slight reddish tinge. The branching pattern creates neat right angles, giving the plant an almost architectural look.

habitat: Look for common centaury in sandy soils near the coast, in disturbed areas, roadsides, and old fields. It prefers well-drained, somewhat poor soils and full sun exposure. In New England, it's most likely to be found in coastal areas from Massachusetts to Maine, often in areas with calcareous (limestone-influenced) soils.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and small rosettes of leaves appear, staying low to the ground for several weeks as the plant builds energy.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from July through August, when the distinctive pink flowers are most visible and the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant produces small capsules filled with tiny seeds before dying back completely as an annual.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain - this annual plant survives only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Common centaury flowers are so sensitive to light that they serve as natural weather predictors - the blooms close tightly before storms and won't open at all on very cloudy days, earning them the folk name 'fair weather friends' in some parts of Europe.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with pink-flowered wild geraniums, but centaury's flowers have exactly 5 flat petals (not the 5 notched petals of geraniums) and grow in tight, flat-topped clusters rather than loose, nodding flowers. Remember: centaury flowers close on cloudy days, while geraniums stay open.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' centaury, this plant is actually quite rare in New England with only 17 recorded observations. The name reflects its abundance in its native Europe, not its status here. It's also sometimes called 'feverfoullie' in older herbals, though this name has largely fallen out of use.
compareHints: Common centaury is larger and more robust than lesser centaury, with flowers arranged in denser, more organized flat-topped clusters rather than loose, branching sprays. Common centaury also has broader leaves and thicker stems, while lesser centaury appears more delicate overall with smaller flowers scattered along branching stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser centaury differs from its cousin common centaury by being much smaller overall and lacking the distinctive flat rosette of leaves that common centaury forms at ground level.
